source_text:
Οὕτω
καὶ τὸν δίκαιον καὶ τὸν ἀσεβῆ διὰ μιᾶς εἰκόνος σχηματίζει ἡ Γραφή· ∆ίκαιος, φησὶν,

ὡς φοῖνιξ ἀνθήσει, ὡς ἡ κέδρος ἡ ἐν τῷ Λιβάνῳ πληθυνθήσεται. Ἐποίησε πρότερον
τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ δικαίου, εἶθ' οὕτως καὶ τοῦ ἀσεβοῦς. Εἶδον γὰρ, φησὶ, τὸν ἀσεβῆ
ὑπερυψούμενον καὶ ἐπαιρόμενον, ὡς τὰς κέδρους τοῦ Λιβάνου. Ὅρα τοίνυν πῶς τὴν
μὲν αὐτὴν εἰκόνα παρήγαγε, ταῖς δὲ λέξεσι τὰς ἐννοίας ἐμέρισεν. Ἐπὶ μὲν γὰρ τοῦ
ἀσεβοῦς λέγει· Εἶδον τὸν ἀσεβῆ ὑπερυψούμενον καὶ ἐπαιρόμενον, ὡς τὰς κέδρους·
ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ δικαίου οὐκ εἶπεν, Ὡσεὶ κέδρος ἡ ἐν τῷ Λιβάνῳ ἐπανθήσεται, ἀλλὰ,
Πληθυνθήσεται. Οὕτως οὖν καὶ τὴν μέλιτταν μίμησαι, ὦ ἄνθρωπε, ἣν καὶ ἡ Γραφὴ
διδάσκει μιμεῖσθαι πρὸς φιλοπονίαν. Πορεύθητι πρὸς τὴν μέλιτταν, καὶ μάθε ὡς
ἐργάτις ἐστί. Μὴ μάθῃς ὅτι κέντρον ἔχει, ἀλλ' ὅτι μέλι ἐργάζεται. Ἐὰν γὰρ μιμήσῃ
τῆς μελίττης τὸ κέντρον, κατηγορεῖ σου ∆αυῒδ, λέγων· Πάντα τὰ ἔθνη ἐκύκλωσάν
με, ὡσεὶ μέλισσαι κηρίον, καὶ τῷ ὀνόματι Κυρίου ἠμυνάμην αὐτούς. Ὁρᾷς πῶς τοὺς
πλήττοντας ἀπεικάζει μελίττῃ πληττούσῃ, τοὺς δὲ δικαίους ἀπεικάζει τῇ τὸ μέλι
ἀποσταζούσῃ; Χείλη γὰρ, φησὶν, ἀνδρῶν δικαίων ἀποστάζουσι σοφίαν· καὶ, Κηρίον
μέλιτος λόγοι καλοί· γλύκασμα δὲ αὐτῶν ἴασις ψυχῆς. Τοῦτο τοίνυν, ἀγαπητοὶ, τὸ
γλύκασμα τῶν ψυχῶν λέγω, ποθήσωμεν ἐξ ὅλης ψυχῆς, καὶ τὸ κηρίον ἐργασώμεθα
τὸ νοερὸν ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ τῆς ψυχῆς ἐργαστηρίῳ, καὶ τὰ θεῖα λόγια λάβωμεν ὑπὲρ
μέλι καὶ κηρίον. Μέλι γὰρ πολὺ ἐσθιόμενον πολλάκις μεταβάλλει τὸ γλύκασμα εἰς
πικρίαν, καὶ διαστρέφει τοῦ στομάχου τὴν ὄρεξιν, καὶ πᾶσαν ἀνασκευάζει τοῦ
ἀνθρώπου τὴν κατάστασιν· λόγος δὲ Θεοῦ λαμβανόμενος πολὺς οὐ θολοῖ τὴν
ψυχὴν, ἀλλὰ θεραπεύει· Γλύκασμα γὰρ αὐτοῦ ἴασις ψυχῆς· ∆ιὰ τοῦτο βουλόμενος ὁ
σοφὸς ἐκεῖνος ἀντιθεῖναι διαφορὰν μέλιτος καὶ λόγου, φησίν· Ἐσθίειν μέλι πολὺ οὐ
καλὸν, τιμᾷν δὲ χρὴ λόγους ἐνδόξους. Ἔχωμεν οὖν, ἀγαπητοὶ, τὸ κηρίον τὸ
ποικίλον, τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἱερὰ λόγια, διὰ παντός· καὶ ὥσπερ τὸ κηρίον ἐκεῖνο ἐκ πολλῶν
μὲν καὶ διαφόρων σχημάτων ἀπαρτίζεται, ἓν δὲ ἔχει καλόν· οὕτω καὶ ἡμῖν ἔστω
κηρίον ἡ θεία Γραφὴ, ἐκ πολλῶν μὲν καὶ διαφόρων συγκειμένη προφητῶν, ἓν δὲ
μέλι διδασκαλίας ἀποστάζουσα. Τοιοῦτον ἡμῖν καὶ τὸ τῶν Πατέρων κηρίον, ἐκ
διαφόρων μὲν ἡλικιῶν συνηρμοσμένον, μίαν δὲ χάριν καὶ μίαν πνευματικὴν
διδασκαλίαν ἀποστάζον. Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν εἰς τοσοῦτον. Γένοιτο δὲ ἡμᾶς εὐχαῖς καὶ
πρεσβείαις τοῦ κοινοῦ Πατρὸς, τῇ φιλοπονίᾳ τὸν λόγον αὔξοντας, τὸν θεῖον
ἀπεργάζεσθαι νόμον ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ πάντοτε, καὶ ποιεῖν ἐκεῖνο τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ ∆αυῒδ
εἰρημένον, τὸ ἔχειν τὸν νόμον τοῦ Θεοῦ πάντοτε ἐν μέσῳ τῆς κοιλίας ἡμῶν, ἤγουν
τὰ θεῖα νοήματα, ὥστε νομίζειν φύσεως ὅρους ἐπιγινώσκειν, τιμᾷν τε τὴν 56.522
ἀλήθειαν, καταφρονεῖν κόσμου, καὶ Θεῷ δόξαν ἀναπέμπειν, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ, καὶ εἰς τοὺς
αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, Ἀμήν.
thought_title: The same image for righteous and wicked and the honey of the divine words
orientation: The preacher shows how Scripture reuses one image with different words for opposite moral meanings and then urges the hearers to imitate only the bee's honey-making diligence.
pass_a_gloss: In this way also Scripture portrays both the righteous man and the impious man by means of one image. 'A righteous man,' it says, 'will bloom like a palm tree, like the cedar in Lebanon he will be multiplied.' It made first the image of the righteous man, then in this way also that of the impious man. 'For I saw,' it says, 'the impious man being exalted and lifting himself up, like the cedars of Lebanon.' See therefore how it brought forward the same image, but by the wordings it divided the meanings. For in the case of the impious man it says: 'I saw the impious man being exalted and lifting himself up, like the cedars'; but in the case of the righteous man it did not say, 'Like a cedar in Lebanon he will bloom again,' but, 'He will be multiplied.' In this way therefore also imitate the bee, O man, which Scripture also teaches to imitate with respect to diligence. 'Go to the bee, and learn how industrious she is.' Do not learn that she has a sting, but that she produces honey. For if you imitate the sting of the bee, David accuses you, saying: 'All the nations encircled me, like bees a honeycomb, and in the name of the Lord I defended myself against them.' Do you see how he likened those who strike to a bee that stings, but likened the righteous to the bee that drips honey? For 'lips,' it says, 'of righteous men drip wisdom'; and, 'Good words are a honeycomb of honey; and their sweetness is healing of soul.' This therefore, beloved, the sweetness of souls I mean, let us desire from all our soul, and let us produce the intelligible honeycomb in the hidden workshop of the soul, and let us take the divine words beyond honey and honeycomb. For honey eaten in much quantity often turns its sweetness into bitterness, and perverts the appetite of the stomach, and overturns the whole condition of the man; but a word of God taken in much quantity does not darken the soul, but heals; for 'its sweetness is healing of soul.' For this reason that wise man, wishing to set against each other the difference of honey and word, says: 'To eat much honey is not good, but one must honor glorious words.' Let us have therefore, beloved, the variegated honeycomb, the divine and holy words, through all time; and just as that honeycomb is put together from many and diverse shapes, but has one good; so also let divine Scripture be for us a honeycomb, composed from many and diverse prophets, but dripping one honey of teaching. Such also for us is the honeycomb of the Fathers, fitted together from diverse ages, but dripping one grace and one spiritual teaching. But these things so far. And may it be that we, by prayers and intercessions of the common Father, increasing the word by diligence, always accomplish the divine law in the mind, and do that which was said by David, to have the law of God always in the midst of our belly, that is the divine thoughts, so as to consider that we recognize the boundaries of nature, and to honor the truth, and to despise the world, and to send up glory to God, now and always, and unto the ages of ages, Amen.

choices.why: keeps literal figure for cedar/bee as scriptural image, not symbol in general
brief glossary sense for φιλοπονία, the ant/bee quality to imitate
brief fixed gloss for κηρίον as image of Scripture and teaching
brief required glossary rendering, sweeter than literal honey

pass_b_english: Scripture portrays both the righteous and the ungodly by means of one image. It says, “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and will be multiplied like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psalm 92:12). It first drew the image of the righteous, and then in the same way the image of the ungodly. For it says, “I saw the ungodly exalted and lifting himself up like the cedars of Lebanon” (Psalm 37:35).

See how it has produced the same image but divided the meanings by its wording. For the ungodly it says, “I saw the ungodly exalted and lifting himself up like the cedars,” while for the righteous it did not say, “He will bloom like a cedar in Lebanon,” but, “He will be multiplied.” So imitate the bee, fellow human, as Scripture itself teaches us to imitate with respect to diligence. Scripture says, “Go to the bee and learn how industrious she is” (Proverbs 6:8).

Learn not that she has a sting, but that she produces honey. If you copy the sting of the bee, David accuses you when he says, “All the nations surrounded me like bees around a honeycomb, and in the name of the Lord I drove them off” (Psalm 118:12). Do you see how he compares those who strike to a bee that stings, but compares the righteous to the bee that drips honey? For Scripture says, “The lips of righteous men drip wisdom” (Proverbs 10:31), and, “Good words are a honeycomb of honey, and their sweetness is healing for the soul” (Proverbs 16:24).

So, beloved, let us long for this sweetness of souls, I mean, with our whole soul. Let us fashion the spiritual honeycomb in the hidden workshop of the soul, and let us take the divine words as sweeter than honey and honeycomb. Much honey eaten often turns its sweetness to bitterness, ruins the stomach’s appetite, and overturns a person’s whole condition. But much of God’s word taken does not cloud the soul; it heals it, for its sweetness is healing for the soul. That wise author wanted to set out the difference between honey and the word, so he says, “Eating much honey is not good, but glorious words must be honored” (Proverbs 25:27).

Let us therefore keep always, beloved, the richly varied honeycomb, the divine and holy words. Just as a honeycomb is built from many different cells yet holds one good, so let divine Scripture be a honeycomb for us, composed from many different prophets yet dripping one honey of teaching. Such for us is also the honeycomb of the Fathers, fitted together from different generations yet dripping one grace and one spiritual teaching. But this is enough on these matters. By the prayers and intercessions of our common Father, may we increase the word by diligence, always carry out the divine law in our mind, and do what David spoke of, holding God’s law always in the midst of our belly, that is, the divine thoughts, so that we make it our rule to recognize the limits of nature, honor truth, despise the world, and send up glory to God, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
notes: '56.522' intruding before ἀλήθειαν is a printed-column marker, not source text to translate.

problems.quote: while for the righteous it did not say the cedar in Lebanon will bloom again, but that it will be multiplied.
problems.source_quote: ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ δικαίου οὐκ εἶπεν, Ὡσεὶ κέδρος ἡ ἐν τῷ Λιβάνῳ ἐπανθήσεται, ἀλλὰ,
problems.why: Omits "like" (ὡσεί), shifting the subject from the righteous person to the cedar itself; also ἐπανθήσεται means "bloom," not "bloom again."
problems.fix: while for the righteous it did not say, “He will bloom like a cedar in Lebanon,” but, “He will be multiplied.”
problems.ruling: Source ὡσεὶ κέδρος ἐπανθήσεται is simile 'like cedar will bloom again'; English drops ὡσεὶ and ἐπαν-, shifting the negated wording.

problems.quote: so that we suppose we discern the limits of nature
problems.why: "Suppose we discern" implies mere assumption or self-deception, absurd in a closing prayer; νομίζειν with an infinitive means "make it our rule/habit" to discern.
problems.fix: so that we make it our rule to discern the limits of nature
problems.ruling: νομίζειν with infinitive means habitually practice, not 'suppose'; closing prayer misstates the intended moral aim.

edits.old: while for the righteous it did not say the cedar in Lebanon will bloom again, but that it will be multiplied.
edits.new: while for the righteous it did not say, “He will bloom like a cedar in Lebanon,” but, “He will be multiplied.”

fixed: agency: fixed omission of ὡσεί and “bloom again” -> “bloom like” to restore righteous person as subject per ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ δικαίου οὐκ εἶπεν, Ὡσεὶ κέδρος...ἐπανθήσεται.

mistranslation — no edit: English “suppose we discern” correctly renders ὥστε νομίζειν φύσεως ὅρους ἐπιγινώσκειν as νομίζειν + infinitive = suppose/consider; customary “make it our rule” is not in the source words.

problems.quote: so that we suppose we discern the limits of nature
problems.why: νομίζειν with an infinitive means to make a practice or rule of doing something, not to 'suppose,' which implies mere assumption in a closing prayer.
problems.fix: so that we make it our rule to recognize the limits of nature
problems.ruling: νομίζειν with ἐπιγινώσκειν denotes habitual practice, not tentative 'suppose'; closing exhortation loses intended moral habit.

edits.old: so that we suppose we discern the limits of nature
edits.new: so that we make it our rule to recognize the limits of nature

fixed: Fixed mistranslation: source ὥστε νομίζειν + ἐπιγινώσκειν, τιμᾶν, καταφρονεῖν, ἀναπέμπειν is customary practice, not supposition.
